title: Hermes invents the tortoise-shell lyre
summary: In the Homeric Hymn to Hermes, Hermes encounters a tortoise, makes a lyre from its shell, and plays it. This is a source-located narrative summary, not a direct quotation.

title: Hermes gives Apollo the lyre in the cattle dispute
summary: In the Homeric Hymn to Hermes, Apollo is delighted by the lyre, and Hermes transfers the instrument to him as part of the reconciliation and exchange involving Apollo’s cattle. This is a source-located summary, not a quotation.

title: Pan plays the syrinx (reed pipes); no lyre use established here
summary: The Homeric Hymn to Pan depicts Pan making music with reed pipes (syrinx). This evidence does not establish lyre playing by Pan; it does not explicitly deny that Pan ever played a lyre. In Ovid’s later Latin account, Syrinx becomes reeds that Pan uses for his pipes. The syrinx is a wind instrument, distinct from the stringed lyre. These are source-located summaries, not collated quotations.
source: Homeric Hymn to Pan 14–27; Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.689–712 (Latin variant)

title: Pan son of Hermes in one tradition
summary: The Homeric Hymn to Pan names Hermes as Pan’s father; other ancient traditions give different parentage. This relationship is tradition-specific, not universal.

title: Orpheus counters Sirens with his music
summary: In Apollonius, Orpheus plays his lyre to overcome the Sirens’ singing during the Argonauts’ voyage. This does not establish that the Sirens themselves played lyres.
